title: Is It Anxiety or Something Else? How to Tell the Difference
description: Your racing heart might be anxiety—or it might be something medical. How to distinguish anxiety from thyroid issues, heart problems, and other conditions that mimic it.

content.text: Racing heart. Shortness of breath. Dizziness. These could be anxiety—or they could be something else entirely. Here's how to tell the difference.

items: Fear of dying or losing control

content.text: Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) causes: rapid heartbeat, sweating, tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance, irritability. A simple blood test (TSH) can rule this out.
Arrhythmias, mitral valve prolapse, and other cardiac issues can cause palpitations and chest discomfort. Key differences from anxiety:

items: Occurs during rest/sleep (anxiety usually has triggers)

content.text: Hypoglycemia causes shakiness, sweating, confusion, rapid heartbeat. Often occurs hours after eating or with diabetes medications.
High caffeine intake mimics anxiety perfectly. Also: energy drinks, pre-workout supplements, ADHD medications, decongestants.
Asthma and COPD can cause breathlessness that triggers (or is mistaken for) anxiety.
Seek emergency care for: chest pain with arm/jaw pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, symptoms during exertion, first-ever panic attack over age 40.

items: You have risk factors for heart disease
Symptoms don't fit the pattern of anxiety
You have other concerning symptoms (weight loss, fever)
You haven't had a physical exam recently

content.text: Tests That Rule Out Medical Causes

items: Basic blood panel (thyroid, blood sugar, electrolytes)

content.text: Here's the tricky part: health anxiety about these symptoms makes them worse. You feel a palpitation, worry it's your heart, which releases adrenaline, which causes more palpitations. Getting medical clearance can break this cycle.

Most anxiety symptoms are anxiety. But if you haven't had a recent physical, or your symptoms are new or atypical, get checked out. Once medical causes are ruled out, you can address the anxiety with confidence—knowing your heart and thyroid are fine.
